title: Nuclear Energy and Radiation
seo_title: Grade 10 Science: Nuclear Energy and Radiation Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Energy is conserved and its transformation can affect living things and the environment: radioactivity, alpha, beta and gamma radiation, half-life, nuclear fission and fusion, and nuclear energy. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 10, Physics)
meta_desc: Free Grade 10 science worksheets (BC): alpha, beta and gamma radiation, nuclear equations, half-life, fission and fusion. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Fission splits nuclei; fusion joins them.
body_html:
How to think about it

Some nuclei are unstable and decay, giving off radiation. Alpha particles (helium nuclei) are stopped by paper, beta particles (electrons) by aluminum, and gamma rays need thick lead or concrete. Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.

In fission a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 splits, releasing a lot of energy (nuclear power plants). In fusion light nuclei such as hydrogen join to form helium, which powers the Sun.

Example

A sample has a half-life of 5 days. What fraction is left after 10 days?

Two half-lives

Answer: 1/4

Example

Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?

The biggest, slowest particle

Answer: alpha

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the whole sample is gone after two half-lives.
  • Mixing up fission and fusion.
  • Thinking gamma rays are particles.

faq.q: Why is fusion hard to use on Earth?
faq.a: It needs extremely high temperatures and pressures.

faq.q: Where is radiation used in medicine?
faq.a: In X-rays, tracers and cancer treatment.

items.q: What is mass defect?
c: the mass of the neutrons only
the difference between the mass of a nucleus and the total mass of its separate nucleons
the mass lost when an atom loses electrons
items.e: It is equivalent to the binding energy.

items.q: Why is technetium-99m good for medical imaging?
c: it emits gamma rays that leave the body and has a short half-life (about 6 hours)
it has a half-life of millions of years
items.e: Short half-life means a low dose.

items.q: What is gamma radiation?
c: high-energy electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus
items.e: It has no charge and no mass.

items.q: What is nuclear fusion?
c: a heavy nucleus splits in two
two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
items.e: Fusion powers the Sun.

items.q: What is a beta-minus particle?
c: a fast electron emitted when a neutron changes into a proton
items.e: The proton number goes up by 1.

items.q: Why do fission and fusion both release energy?
c: the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon, so mass is converted to energy (E = mc²)
items.e: The mass defect becomes energy.

items.q: What is nuclear fission?
c: a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons
a nucleus emits only gamma rays
items.e: Fission is used in nuclear reactors.

items.q: A nucleus has 79 protons and 73 neutrons. It undergoes beta decay. How many neutrons does the new nucleus have?
items.e: A neutron changes into a proton.

items.q: A nucleus with atomic number 89 undergoes beta decay. What is the new atomic number?

items.q: Which radiation needs several centimetres of lead to reduce it greatly?
items.e: Gamma is the most penetrating.

items.q: What is a chain reaction?
c: neutrons from one fission cause further fissions
alpha particles join to make heavier nuclei
a reaction that needs no fuel
electrons cause atoms to ionize one after another
items.e: Control rods absorb neutrons to control the rate.

items.q: Which nucleus has the highest binding energy per nucleon?
c: iron-56 (near the peak of the curve)
items.e: Nuclei lighter than iron can release energy by fusion; heavier ones by fission.

items.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
items.e: Alpha is the most ionizing and least penetrating.

items.q: Why is alpha radiation most dangerous inside the body?
c: it is stopped by skin outside the body, so it is safe inside
it passes straight through the body
it is very ionizing and all its energy is absorbed by nearby cells
items.e: Outside the body skin stops it.

items.q: Which radiation is the most strongly ionizing?
items.e: Its large charge and mass cause many ionizations.

items.q: The half-life of cesium-137 is 30 years. A sample has an activity of 4000 Bq. What is its activity after 90 years?
items.e: 90 years is 3 half-lives: 4000 ÷ 23 = 500 Bq.

items.q: What is gamma radiation?

electromagnetic radiation of very short wavelength

items.q: What is nuclear fusion?
c: the decay of a nucleus by alpha emission
the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
the splitting of a heavy nucleus
items.e: It powers the Sun.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for sterilizing medical instruments?

items.q: What is needed to absorb most beta radiation?
c: a few cm of air or a sheet of paper
several cm of lead or thick concrete (reduced, not completely)
items.e: Penetration: alpha < beta < gamma.

items.q: What is the relative charge of gamma radiation?
items.e: Alpha +2, beta −1, gamma 0 (uncharged).

items.q: What is nuclear fission?
c: the splitting of a large nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons
items.e: Used in nuclear power plants.

items.q: What is background radiation?
c: radiation only from nuclear power plants
low-level radiation that is always present from natural and artificial sources
items.e: Subtract it from readings.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for detecting leaks in underground water pipes?

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for killing cancer cells (radiotherapy) from outside the body?

items.q: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
items.e: Gamma rays are uncharged and weakly ionizing.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for a smoke detector?
items.e: Alpha particles ionize air between two plates; smoke absorbs them and the current falls, setting off the alarm.

items.q: Why is ionizing radiation harmful to living cells?
c: It can damage DNA, killing cells or causing mutations that may lead to cancer.
items.e: Ionization breaks molecules.

items.q: Why is radioactive decay described as random?
c: It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when.
It happens at the same time for all nuclei.
items.e: Only the rate for a large number can be predicted.

items.q: What is alpha radiation?
c: electromagnetic radiation of very short wavelength
a fast-moving electron from the nucleus
items.e: Alpha: He nucleus. Beta: electron. Gamma: EM wave.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for a medical tracer injected into the body?
items.e: Gamma passes out of the body to a detector and is weakly ionizing.

items.q: Which type of radiation is used for controlling the thickness of paper or aluminum foil?
items.e: The amount of beta getting through changes with thickness; alpha would be stopped and gamma would hardly change.

items.q: How ionizing is alpha radiation?
items.e: Ionizing power: alpha > beta > gamma.

items.q: What happens to the proton number in alpha decay?
items.e: The nucleon number decreases by 4.

items.e: Alpha +2, beta −1, gamma 0 (uncharged).
